comparing-distributions-s1.title: Travel times on two bus routes
comparing-distributions-s1.text: A commuter timed 15 trips on each of two bus routes from her home to work, in minutes. Route 1: 24, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 30, 31, 32, 33, 33, 34, 35, 37, 39. Route 2: 18, 20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38, 41, 45, 62 (invented data).

plot.label: Parallel boxplots of travel times in minutes for two bus routes, 15 trips each. Route 1: box from 28 to 34, median 31, whiskers from 24 to 39. Route 2: box from 23 to 38, median 28, whiskers from 18 to 45, one outlier at 62.

comparing-distributions-s2.title: Scores in two chemistry classes
comparing-distributions-s2.text: Two chemistry classes took different tests. Ana, in class A, scored 86. Ben, in class B, scored 88 (invented data).

items.q: Which statement compares the centers of the two distributions?

why.correct: Compare with a comparing word and numbers: Route 1’s median (31) is greater than Route 2’s (28).
options: Both numbers are right, but a comparison needs a comparing word: which median is greater?
Right: it names both medians and says which is greater, in context.
The longest trip is not the center. Route 2’s median, 28, is the smaller one.
The medians differ by 3 minutes, and the comparison should say which is greater.
The median travel time for Route 1 is 31 minutes, and the median for Route 2 is 28 minutes
Route 1 has a greater median travel time (31 minutes) than Route 2 (28 minutes)
Route 2 has the greater center, as its trips run up to 62 minutes
The routes have about the same center, as both are about 30 minutes

items.q: Which statement compares the variability of the two routes?

why.correct: Compare spreads with a measure such as the IQR: 15 minutes for Route 2 against 6 for Route 1, so Route 2 is more variable.
options: A larger center says nothing about spread.
Equal sample sizes do not mean equal spread.
Where the box starts is position, not spread; Route 2’s box is wider.
Right: Route 2’s box is much wider, $38 - 23 = 15$ against $34 - 28 = 6$.
Route 1’s times vary more, since its median of 31 minutes is the greater of the two medians
The routes vary equally, since each has 15 timed trips
Route 2’s times vary less, since its box starts at a lower time
Route 2’s times vary more: its IQR is 15 minutes, against 6 for Route 1

items.q: Which comparison is the most complete?

why.correct: A complete comparison covers shape, center, spread and unusual features, each with a comparing word and numbers, in context.
options: Right: shape, outliers, center and spread are all compared, with numbers and comparing words, in context.
The numbers are right, but nothing is compared: which is greater, which varies more?
"Better" and "worse" are judgments; the comparison needs shape, center and spread.
This ignores the outlier, the different medians and the very different spreads.

Route 2 is skewed right with an outlier at 62 minutes, while Route 1 is roughly symmetric with none; Route 1 has the greater median (31 against 28) but much less variability (IQR 6 against 15 minutes)
Route 1’s median is 31 and its IQR is 6; Route 2’s median is 28 and its IQR is 15, and Route 2 also has an outlier at 62 minutes
Route 2 is better, because some of its trips are much faster, and Route 1 is worse, because its trips are slower on most days
Both routes have trips from about 20 to about 40 minutes, so the two distributions are nearly the same

items.q: The commuter must reach work within 40 minutes every day. Which route should she choose, based on these trips?

why.correct: The claim is about the longest trips, so look at the upper end: Route 1 never went over 39 minutes; Route 2 went over 40 three times.
options: A lower typical time does not help if some trips are too long; 3 of Route 2’s trips took over 40 minutes.
Her need is to never be late, which depends on the longest trips.
Right: Route 1’s maximum is 39. Route 2 took longer than 40 minutes on 3 of its 15 trips.
Medians under 40 still allow trips over 40; Route 2 had three.
Route 2: its median of 28 minutes is lower than Route 1’s
Route 2: its fastest trip, 18 minutes, beats any Route 1 trip
Route 1: all 15 of its trips took 39 minutes or less
Either route

items.q: Type the expression for the z-score of Ana’s score of 86 in class A.

mistakes.why: Subtract in the order value minus mean, so a score above the mean has a positive z-score: (86 − 74)/8.
Put brackets around the subtraction: (86 − 74)/8. Without them only 74 is divided by 8.

items.q: Type the expression for the z-score of Ben’s score of 88 in class B.

mistakes.why: Use Ben’s own class: its standard deviation is 4, not 8.
Use class B’s mean, 81, for Ben.

items.q: Which student did better compared with their own class?

why.correct: Standardize: Ana $z = 1.5$, Ben $z = 1.75$. Ben is further above his class in standard deviation units.
options: Raw distances ignore spread. Class B’s scores vary less, so 7 points there is a bigger achievement.
The classes took different tests, so raw scores cannot be compared.
Right: Ben’s score is farther above his class mean, measured in standard deviations.
z-scores are made exactly for this: they put both scores on the same scale.
Ana: her score is 12 points above her class mean, and Ben’s is 7
Ben, because his score of 88 is higher than Ana’s 86
Ben: his z-score of 1.75 is higher than Ana’s 1.5
Neither

items.q: Interpret Ana’s z-score of 1.5 in context.

why.correct: A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean, in context.

size.label: How far
options: 1.5 standard deviations
1.5 points
1.5 percent

why.1: A z-score counts standard deviations, not points.
why.2: A z-score is not a percent.

options: above
below

why.1: A positive z-score means above the mean.

context.label: Compared with
options: the mean score of class A
the median score of class A
the top score in class A

why.1: A z-score measures from the mean.
why.2: A z-score measures from the mean, not the top score.

conclude.model: Ana’s score of 86 is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean score of class A.

items.q: A runner’s time has a z-score of $-2$ among runners in her race. What does this mean?

why.correct: Negative z: below the mean. $|z| = 2$: two standard deviations away.
options: Right: a negative z-score is below the mean; the size counts standard deviations.
A z-score counts standard deviations, not minutes.
A z-score gives distance from the mean, not a place in the order.
A z-score is not a percent.
Her time is 2 standard deviations below the mean time
Her time is 2 minutes faster than the mean time in the race
She finished in second place among the runners
Her time is 2% lower than the mean time in the race

items.q: Scores on a quiz have mean 60 and standard deviation 10. What score has a z-score of $-0.5$?

why.correct: Undo the z-score: value = mean + z × SD = $60 + (-0.5)(10) = 55$.
options: A negative z-score is below the mean.
z counts standard deviations: subtract $0.5 \times 10 = 5$.
z is $-0.5$, half a standard deviation.

items.q: In one school the median commute is 20 minutes; in another it is 30 minutes. A student says the median commute for both schools together must be 25 minutes. Is that right?

why.correct: You cannot average medians to get the median of combined data; it depends on every value and on the group sizes.
options: That holds only in special cases. With 1,000 students at one school and 100 at the other, the larger school dominates.
Right: a median of combined data comes from all the values together; averaging two medians usually gives the wrong answer.
Even symmetric groups of different sizes give a combined median closer to the larger group’s.
It can be anywhere from 20 to 30, depending on the data.
Yes: the median of the combined data is the average of the two medians
No: it depends on each school’s size and on all the values
Yes, as long as each of the two schools has a symmetric distribution
No: it is 30 minutes

items.q: Distribution A of reaction times is roughly symmetric; distribution B is skewed right. Which statement about their shapes is a correct comparison?

why.correct: Compare shapes directly: B has a long tail toward larger (slower) times; A does not.
options: Right: right skew in B means a few much slower reaction times that A does not have.
Shape says nothing about the number of values.
Skew alone does not tell which center is greater; that needs the centers themselves.
Both may be unimodal, but one is symmetric and the other skewed.
B has a longer tail toward slow times than A does
A has more reaction times than B, since it is symmetric
B has a greater center than A, since it is skewed right
A and B have the same shape

items.q: Kai’s height is at the 90th percentile of his class. Lena’s is at the 85th percentile of hers. What does this tell you?

why.correct: Percentiles and z-scores describe relative position within a group, not raw size across groups.
options: Percentiles are relative to each class; Lena could be taller in centimeters.
A percentile is a position, not a measurement.
Right: a percentile gives relative position within the person’s own group.
Percentiles inside each class say nothing about which class is taller.
Kai is taller than Lena, since 90 is more than 85
Kai is 90 cm tall and Lena is 85 cm tall
Kai is taller than 90% of his class, and Lena than 85% of hers
Kai’s class is taller than Lena’s on average

items.q: Which of these describe the relative position of a value in its distribution? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Percentiles and z-scores are measures of relative position.
options: Right: it counts standard deviations above or below the mean.
Right: it gives the percent of values at or below it.
The range describes the whole distribution’s spread, not one value’s position.
The sample size says nothing about where one value stands.
Its z-score
Its percentile
The range of the data
The number of values in the data

items.q: Heights of a team are measured in inches and the z-score of one player is 1.2. If the heights are converted to centimeters, what is the player’s z-score?

why.correct: A z-score has no units: $\frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}$ has the same units on top and bottom, so changing units leaves it unchanged.
options: The top and bottom of the z-score both get multiplied by 2.54, so it cancels.
Right: converting units multiplies the value, the mean and the standard deviation by 2.54, so the ratio is unchanged.
Nothing is divided: the change in units cancels out.
Whatever the height, the z-score stays 1.2: it has no units.
Still 1.2
It depends on the player’s height in centimeters

items.q: Two dotplots: weights of apples from orchard A run from 150 to 170 grams; weights from orchard B run from 120 to 210 grams. Both are centered near 160 grams. Which statement is a correct comparison?

why.correct: With similar centers, compare spread: B’s weights cover a far wider range, so B is more variable.
options: The centers are similar; B also has much lighter apples.
Values close together mean less variability.
Same center, very different spread.
Right: B’s weights spread over 90 grams, A’s over 20, with similar centers.
Orchard B’s apples are heavier, since some weigh 210 grams
Orchard A’s apples are more variable, since they are close together
The orchards are the same, since both centers are near 160 grams
The weights from orchard B are more variable than those from A
